notes.meaning: Parents were told to explain to their children that this meal honored the Lord for shielding their families. Even before their rescue took place, the people bowed down in humble worship to thank God for His promise. They accepted the meal as both a duty and a great privilege.

The people went home and carried out every instruction God gave to Moses and Aaron. Their deliverance depended on real obedience, not just agreeing with the message in their minds. By faith, they put the blood on their doors and prepared the meal.

At midnight, the Lord struck down every firstborn male across Egypt, from Pharaoh's heir to the prisoner in the deepest cell. The judgment also took the firstborn of their farm animals. God showed that rank offered no shelter against His holy anger.

Pharaoh, his officials, and ordinary citizens woke up in the dark to find death in almost every house. A bitter cry arose across the land as families discovered their loss. The Egyptians were famous for loud, intense mourning, and grief fell on everyone at once.

In sheer terror, Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron by night and ordered the Israelites to leave immediately. He surrendered every point he had argued over, telling them to take all their people and livestock to worship God. Broken in spirit, the king even begged Moses to pray for a blessing on him.

The Egyptian people begged the Israelites to hurry and leave the country. They were terrified that any delay would cause everyone in Egypt to drop dead. When people face death so closely, it makes them realize how fragile their own lives are.

Because the Egyptians rushed them out, the Israelites had no time to let yeast work into their bread dough. They packed their lightweight kneading bowls and raw dough into their outer cloaks and slung them over their shoulders. God had planned for them to eat flat bread, and their sudden exit made it a practical necessity.

The Israelites asked their Egyptian neighbors for silver, gold, and fine clothing, and the Lord moved the Egyptians to give them whatever they requested. This was not stealing; it was God providing back pay for centuries of unpaid slave labor. Israel marched out like a victorious army carrying the spoils of war.

The people set out on foot from Rameses toward their first campsite at Succoth. The group included around 600,000 grown men capable of soldiering, which pointed to an entire community of over two million people including women and children. God had multiplied Jacob's small family into a huge nation, keeping His ancient promise.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that 600,000 may represent military squads or symbolic numbers rather than a literal count of fighting men, given the extreme logistical hurdles of moving over two million people at once.

notes.meaning: A large crowd of non-Israelites went with them, along with vast herds of livestock. Some of these outsiders may have been impressed by God's power during the plagues, while others were foreign slaves seizing a chance to run away. Large herds are mentioned because Pharaoh had tried so hard to keep their animals behind.

At their camp, the Israelites baked flat, unleavened loaves from the dough they carried out of Egypt. They had been driven out so fast that they could not pack ordinary travel supplies. Their emergency provisions became an ongoing reminder of how swiftly the Lord had rescued them.

Israel's stay away from their promised home reached 430 years, and they marched out on the exact anniversary date God had planned. The Lord organized His rescued people into orderly ranks like disciplined troops rather than a disorganized mob. God never forgets His timing or His promises.

The Lord stayed awake and watched over Israel throughout that night to bring them safely out of bondage. In return, all future generations of Israelites were commanded to stay watchful and honor the Lord on this sacred night every year. It marked the great birthday of their nation.

The Lord gave Moses and Aaron specific rules about who could take part in the Passover meal, stating that no foreigner could eat it. This boundary protected the meal from being treated like an ordinary dinner by people who did not worship the true God. The feast belonged only to those in covenant fellowship with the Lord.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary sees the Passover as a picture of Holy Communion, which is reserved only for baptized believers in full fellowship with the Church.

notes.meaning: A purchased servant could join the meal only after undergoing circumcision, which was the physical sign of joining God's covenant family. Once circumcised, the servant received the very same religious standing and privileges as his master. God showed that belonging to His family was based on covenant commitment, not social standing.

A short-term traveler or a hired worker was barred from eating the Passover lamb. Hired laborers and visitors had not joined the covenant household, so they could not claim its covenant meal. Sharing the feast required full belonging, not just working alongside God's people.

The lamb had to be eaten inside a single house, none of the meat could be taken outside, and not a single bone could be broken. Eating inside kept the family safe behind the blood on the doorposts and symbolized unity among God's people. Roasting the lamb whole pointed ahead to Jesus, whose bones were not broken when He died on the cross.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The lamb eaten whole inside one house prefigures the holy sacrifice of the Eucharist, received by the faithful within the unity of the church without dividing Christ.

notes.meaning: The whole community of Israel was required to celebrate the Passover together. Even though each household gathered in its own home, the feast was an act of the entire congregation standing as one. No member of God's saved people was allowed to ignore this memorial.

If a resident foreigner wished to join the Passover, every male in his home had to be circumcised first, giving him the exact same rights as a native-born Israelite. God applied one single standard to everyone, welcoming outsiders into His covenant on the same terms. This opened an early door of grace for people of all nations to know the Lord.

All the Israelites followed the Lord's commands exactly as Moses and Aaron delivered them. Amid midnight panic and hasty packing, God gave His people calm hearts and ready hands to obey. Their prompt faith kept them safe and ready for the march.

On that exact day, the Lord led the children of Israel out of Egypt organized by their tribal divisions. They moved forward not as scattered runaway slaves, but as God's orderly army under His personal command. Every promise God had made about their rescue came completely true.
